speechtext:
I -was speaking of the great organization necessary in connection with so large a force as that which Canada is maintaining in this war. I omitted, a reference to the Canadian Dental Service which, as I am informed by the officers of the Department of Militia and Defence, has made it possible for about fifty thousand Canadians to pass the examination and to enter military service who otherwise might have been unable-probably would have been unable-to do so. Canada was one of the first countries in the world to establish this service, and the results which have been obtained are eminently satisfactory in every way.
If I may be permitted to allude to some other departments of the Government upon which unusual burdens have been cast in this war, I would mention the Naval Service. The coast defence of this country has been largely under the control of that department. It is perfectly true that in the early months of the war, when we consulted the British Government, we wer asked to concentrate our efforts upon military organization and to leave the question of naval defence to the Admiralty. Nevertheless, it has been necessary to establish patrols, and a number of patrol boats have been secured by the department; I should not Ibe surprised if such efforts must engage their attention still more in the future. That department has had charge of the closing and guarding of our harbours and of the censorship of wireless stations. Upon that department also has devolved the duty of establishing and maintaining naval bases upon a war footing on both coasts, which bases have been utilized not only for the ships of the British Navy but for the ships of allied navies as well. The training of the officers and men who have enlisted has also been a matter of serious import for the Minister and officers of that department. They have kept in constant touch with the Admiralty in these matters. Further, the Minister of Naval Service has beep chairman of the sub-committee of Council which has had charge of arrangements respecting the Admiralty transport. I shall speak of that more later on, as in that connection highly important duties have been imposed upon the Minister of the Naval Service.
It would be undesirable for me to omit allusion to the fact that the production of munitions in this war is quite as important as the enlistment of men. I have said before, and now repeat, that this is a war in which applied science and applied mechanics play a part as important as the armies themselves. It has been, recently stated by the chairman of the Imperial Munitions Board, and I have no doubt that the .statement is correct, that Canada is to-day producing more munitions of war than any country produced before the war, with the single exception of Germany. To give an idea of the magnitude that these operations have assumed, I am informed by the chairman of the Imperial Munitions Board that the workmen and inspectors engaged in these operations at the present time number more than 304,000; that there are 630 factories, chemical plants and loading stations which are producing or otherwise dealing with munitions; and that the orders, including the expenditure for an aeroplane factory which is in progress, and including also the anticipated orders for aeroplanes, exceed $700,000,000. It is a very gratifying thing to the people

of this country, and I know to the gentlemen of this House, to know that $250,000, 000 has been provided in Canada for the purpose of enabling this work to be done. Of this sum, $100,000,000 has been provided by the banks of Canada. I desire to pay a tribute of appreciation to the banks for their splendid co-operation in making that provision, and in other matters connected with the carrying on of the war. The balance, $150,000,000 has been provided by the Government of Canada, and it is anticipated that arrangements can be made which will enable the Government of Canada to provide further large sums for this purpose in the future. If we are to have munitions produced on a great scale in Canada, we must make some provision ourselves to assist the British Government in financing those arrangements. There has been the most hearty co-operation between the Government of Canada and the Government of the United Kingdom for this purpose, and that co-operation will continue to the end.
The .production of copper, zinc and lead has been encouraged through the production of munitions, and important tonnage has been created. All the cartridge oases and fuses are being manufactured in Canada today, I understand. One very gratifying feature, which gave me some surprise considering the enormous extent of the orders, is that ninety per cent of the steel necessary for this purpose in the year 1917 will be produed in Canada. That is a great tribute to the management of the steel industries of Canada, because it is obvious to all the members of this House that the requirements of steel for the production of so enormous a quantity of munitions must be very great indeed and far beyond what would have been possible in this country under ordinary conditions.
The production of gun cotton and of the necessary acids for the manufacture of nitrocellulose powdeT, acetone, and many other important articles requisite for munitions, including tri-nitro-toluol, has been firmly established- I could speak iat great length on what has been accomplished in the production of munitions in this country, but the subject 'has been very fully dealt with by the chairman of the Imperial Munitions Board in recent utterances.
Another very important matter which the department of the Government have dealt with is the execution of vast orders from the British and Allied Governments, and from the Governments of New Zealand

and South Africa. I have not an exact statement of the amount to which those orders have run; certainly it is not less that $150,000,000, and probably well up to $200,000,000. The departments which have been charged with the execution of these orders are the Department of Militia ana Defence, the Department of Trade and Commerce -and the Department of Agriculture. Remember, Mr. Speaker, if you please, that the execution of even a million' dollar order, involving contracts with, perhaps, 40, 50 or 100 people all over this country, -and involving -also inspection of articles produced and arangements for their transportation-all this imposes-an enormous amount of administrative and executive work upon any department of the Government that undertakes it. Consider also the enormous variety of articles which have been purchased in this, way: army blankets, artillery harness, gun carriages, limbers, railway oars, saddlery, knitted goods, wheat, flour, o-ats, bay, and supplies of all kinds. When lion, gentlemen realize that those orders run into $150,000,000 or $200,000,000 and that they involve a very large organization, constant supervision and frequent negotiations with the governments for whom the various departments are -acting, they will understand that -all this has entailed .an enormous amount of labour and responsibility upon the departments that have been actively concerned.
I should allude also to the work of the War Purchasing Commission. It was established, as hon. gentlemen know, in May, 1915, for the purpose of purchasing in the most effective way and with the least opportunity for waste or maladministration all supplies required by any department of the Government in connection with or for the purpose of the war. Nearly every department of the Government has purchased supplies in that way: the Department of Militia and Defence and the Department of Naval Service are naturally the two principal departments-but the Department of Justice in connection with internment operations, and other departments of the Government from time to time apply to the commission as they may require articles which are properly chargeable against the war appropriation. The War Purchasing Commission makes these purchases by tender and contract, unless in exceptional cases, for reasons stated in writing. Some time ago its purchases had aggregated more than $80,000,000. I do not know what they would amount to at the present time-con-

siderably in excess of that figure. A great organization has been created and the business has, as I believe, been conducted with very great efficiency. The grateful thanks of this country are due to the three gentlemen who, without any remuneration and purely as a duty of public service, have devoted their time and their energies for almost two years, to carrying on the work of that commission.
Another subject has engaged the attention of the Government. Two years ago we took up with the Admiralty the very important question of transportation. We all remember how great the difficulties were at the time. It seemed to me that the best course would be to despatch a gentleman of great experience in these matters to Great Britain and endeavour to have him come to arrangements with the Admiralty by which the problem of transportation might be -dealt with in a systematic and effective way. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, a corporation which has rendered great service to the Government of the United Kingdom as well as to this Government in matters connected with the war, freely and voluntarily placed at the disposal of the Government the services of Mr. A. H. Harris. Without effective organization of some kind, matters were bound to get into the most extreme confusion. There was the question of transporting supplies and munitions for the British Government, as well as for the Allied Governments, and connected with all this was the question of transporting the general products of the country which were to find a market on the other side of the ocean. The organization was begun in -a very small way-I think with ten or twelve ships in the first instance. That was twb years ago; the organization now includes seventy-five ocean steamers under the able and efficient direction of Mr. A. H. Harris as Canadian director of overseas transports. The organization handles 2,250,000 tons per year and the traffic is constantly increasing. The organization is carried on under a committee of the Privy Council over which the Minister of Nav-al Service presides.
I know that hon. gentlemen of this House will realize that very unusual responsibilities and burdens have been imposed upon the Minister of Finance and his officers during this war. He will no doubt, at a later date, speak more fully on that subject than it would be possible for me to do tonight. For two years he has maintained the finances of Canada without resorting to the British market, which has thus been left
free to sustain the burdens imposed by the enormous British war expenditure and the requirements of the Allies. I do not believe that any one of us would have believed two and a half years ago that it would be possible for Canada to accomplish the task which has been accomplished under the direction of the Minister of Finance in that respect. The two loans placed in Canada have attained an unprecedented success, the one for $50,000,000 bringing out $110,000,000, and the further loan of $100,000,000 being more than doubly subscribed. Not only has the minister been enabled to leave the British market free for the enormous requirements of the British and the Allied Governments, but he has out of the loans which he has effected in Canada put no less than $150,000,000 at the disposal of the British Government for the purpose of paying for the munitions produced in this country. As I have said, that effort will be continued by him in 'the future.	[DOT]
Hon. gentlemen of the House will remember that at the commencement of this war we were faced with very grave conditions indeed in Canada.	-
I do not think that those of my colleagues who were in Ottawa on the first, second and third days of August, 1914, will ever forget the tremendous importance of the problems with which we were faced and the very great responsibilities which we had to assume at that time.
The people of Canada were beginning to think of drawing their money out of the banks in gold. We were threatened with a condition that might have produced a panic which would have paralysed) the energies of Canada in this war. Without any legal power, without any legal sanction to do it, we were obliged to take measures which were afterwards ratified by Parliament. We were obliged to prevent the exportation and hoarding of gold. We were obliged to make bank notes good legal tender. We were obliged to provide that Dominion notes need not be redeemed in gold. These measures were accepted unhesitatingly by the country. No one except those who underwent the responsibilities of that time can properly estimate what might have been the loss to this country if those measures had not been taken.
Then we were faced almost immediately afterwards with another very serious problem. I would like the House and the country to realize for a moment what the conditions were at that time. The revenues of this country had shrunk-I do not know by what percentage-'-but they had shrunk



enormously immediately after the outbreak of the war. Trade was almost paralysed; importation almost stopped, and exportation as well, and in the midst of that we found ourselves confronted with a very serious condition in a very large district in western Canada, in the provinces, of Saskatchewan and Alberta, a district much larger than some of the other provinces of Canada. There was this condition confronting us: the revenues of the country, as my honourable friend the Minister of Finance graphically described them, were shot to pieces on the one hand, and on the other hand there was the need for some assistance to the people in that drought-stricken district. We had the alternative, to display a lack of courage and to say that, confronted by a war such as was upon us, with shrunken revenues, it would be impossible for the Government to. do anything, or, to attack the problem in a courageous way and do what we could to relieve the situation. We determined to relieve the situation and we spent $12,000,000 in providing supplies for the people, fodder for their cattle, and seed grain. I believe that seven and a half million dollars' worth of seed grain went into that district in the following spring. It required some courage to do that, and I venture to. s.ay that this expenditure of $12,000,000 so made by the Government has brought in at least $100,000,000 of wealth and has maintained a happy, prosperous, confident population in a district which otherwise would have been partially depopulated; and I believe that practically every dollar of that money will he paid back. It was not handed out as' a gift; it wias handed out as a loan by this parliament. Gentlemen from the West who are not affiliated with the party to which I belong have concurred with me that probably one hundred million dollars' worth of production had resulted from the action of the Government on that occasion. I am not speaking of this in any boastful way; we did it because it was our duty to do it, and if we had lacked' the courage to undertake it at that time we would not have been fit for the positions we hold. I have spoken of its direct benefit to the country, and indirectly it has. .been of enormous, advantage, because of the splendid production in that very district not only last year, but this year as well. Confidence has bean re-established. Conditions such as occurred in 1914 are of very infrequent occurrence, and the people of that district may con-
tinue in their work of progress and development without undue apprehension.
There is another consideration which I would like to impress upon the House and the country. The commercial and financial stability of Canada during the past two years have been maintained to an extent which was not anticipated by the most optimistic among us two and a half years ago. That has been largely due to two considerations: first, to the abundant crops of the first year, and the high prices obtained therefor, and- the still higher .prices realized for the less abundant crop of the past year. It is due also to the vast orders for munitions and supplies of various kinds which have come to Canada as a land of great production, and of great possibilities. Without wearying the House with figures, let me allude to the conditions which we find at the close of 1916. The total trade of the country for the twelve months ending 31st December, 1916,-I am including coin and bullion-was as follows: imports, $766,733,991; exports, $1,091,706,403, or a total trade for Canada of $1,850,440,394. I do not wish to be understood as attaching too much importance to these figures. I realize, of course, that a considerable proportion of this amount is due to the higher prices which have been obtained. I realize that a considerable amount of it is due to the production of munitions of war which we cannot expect to continue after the war is over. But even with all these qualifications, it is a remarkable result. I remember when I had been in this House for, I think, four years, in 1900 or 1901, the late Sir Richard Cartwright spoke proudly of the fact that the total trade of this country was approaching the four hundred million mark. I remember precisely his expression -the four hundred million mark. The total trade of this country to-day is approaching the two thousand million mark, and it is very likely that by the 31st of March next it will reach that figure, because I observe that during the first nine months of the present fiscal year, that is the nine months beginning on the 1st day of April and ending on the 31st December last, the total trade of Canada was $1,464,503,766, embracing: imports, $602,873,953, and exports $861,629,813. It is a gratifying feature that the exports of Canada have shown a very large increase over the imports.
For the twelve months ended December 31, 1916, the excess of exports over imports was about $325,000,000, and for the nine months of that period ending December 31, 1916, it was $259,000,000. It will be observed, and it is worthy of note, that the exporta-

tion of Canadian products during the first nine months of the present fiscal year exceeded by $300,000,000 the total trade of this country ten years ago. That is a remarkable fact. It indicates that under war conditions the stability and production of the country have been maintained. It is a tribute to the productive power of this country, the industry, activity and enterprise of the people and their ability to take advantage of their opportunities for production.
Now, there are some other departments of the Government that have had unusual duties to perform as well. The Minister of Justice has taken charge of the internment of alien enemies, and he has established camps in various parts of the country. He and the officers of his department have been charged with enforcing the regulations respecting the possession of arms by persons of enemy nationality who are resident in Canada. At the internment camps, which have been established in different parts of the country, work has been provided and from time to time, as labour conditions seemed to render it necessary, aliens, whose character and conduct had been unexceptionable, and who were of good will, have been permitted to engage in the ordinary activities of the country and to earn their own livelihood. In connection with that, I should observe that two camps which I had the opportunity of seeing during my recent tour in aid of National Service, one situated [DOT] in the northern part of the province of Quebec and the other in the northern part of the province of Ontario, are, as I understand, to be utilized as experimental and demonstration farms, and that the district where they are situate is of a character to indicate that settlement on a considerable scale may be expected there when once it has been shown, as it will be shown by these demonstration farms, that the opportunities for profitable agriculture are very advantageous.
The Royal Northwest Mounted Police have had very important, and somewhat unusual, duties to perform in connection with the war. I do not think too much credit can be given for the good work which that force has done. They have had to use tact and firmness, and the results in certain communities in western Canada, where one might expect some unrest, have been on the whole all that could be expected or even desired.
The Department of Customs has been charged with the recommendation and
enforcement of regulations respecting the exportation of articles useful in connection with the war. An enormous amount of responsibility has been imposed on the Government, and chiefly upon the Minister of Customs and his officials, in this respect. There is scarcely a day, and certainly not a week, in which some subject in this connection has not to be taken up. The object, of course, is -to restrict to allied countries the exportation of articles which may be of use to the enemy in connection with the war, and to restrict as much as possible the exportation of these articles under any conditions in which they might become of use to the enemy. In the same way questions have sometimes come up with respect to the importation of articles which were of enemy origin in the first instance, hut which are absolutely necessary for the maintenance of some Canadian industry essential to the war. All these questions have had to be carefully considered. We have had to take a great many of them up with the British Government, and in all cases the course which we have taken has been in full co-operation with, and has received the approval of, the British Government.
The withdrawal of a very large number of men from industrial activities has sometimes created difficult conditions in regard to labour, its employment and remuneration. I think a very just tribute should be paid to the labour men of Canada in connection with their attitude in such matters. There has been very little industrial disturbance considering the amount which has taken place in some other countries. The Minister of Labour has had unusually severe responsibilities imposed upon him. The Minister of Public Works has ably cooperated on many occasions with the Minister of Labour and has fully shared these responsibilities. The Minister of Labour has also been charged with duties under the provisions of the law which forbid combination to raise prices and the hoarding of commodities for the like purpose. As far Ss I understand the situation, these two elements are the only ones which the Government can effectually deal with, as conditions created by the war cannot, .of course, be controlled by any governmental action.
Then, in common with all the railway systems of the country, the Canadian Government Railways have.. had to undertake the vastly increased business created by war conditions. They have transported
300,000	soldiers in Canada since the war broke out, and they have done that without any accident.
Far more than that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend the late Minister of Militia and Defence thinks that the estimate that I have given of the number of soldiers transported is too low. I have taken this from some source- I cannot quite remember what. Hospital trains have been established on the Intercolonial Railway for wounded soldiers in connection with the Military Hospitals Commission. The Canadian Government railways have 'Carried more than 250,000 tons of munitions and war stores to St. John and Halifax, and the equipment at St. John and Halifax has been very greatly improved to render possible the handling of the increased monthly tonnage. They have undertaken during the winter months to carry
60,000	tons a month to one port and 20,000 to the other.
A hundred thousand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The tonnage which they have undertaken to transport to the ports of Halifax and St. John during the winter is 100,000 tons per month. It has been necessary to make extensions in the yards and various other improvements at the terminals and at other points and the three new berths at Halifax have been assigned to Canadian overseas transport and will be fully occupied.
Now, I could speak of the work which has been performed, and is being performed, by every department of the Government. I should not omit to mention that which has been undertaken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He has made successful efforts for the use of articles for which there was no ready market. He has undertaken a work of research preparatory to the conditions which will confront us when the war is concluded. He has sent officers specially trained for the purpose into some countries where we might expect to find wider markets in the future, and he has occupied himself generally in the task of inducing the producers of Canada to take into account the conditions which will confront this country when peace shall have been concluded.
I would like to impress upon hon. gentlemen in this House the importance of our realizing those conditions. I shall not speak fully upon this subject to-night. It is possible that some opportunity may come later on when it will be proper to give it more consideration. We shall have to consider the demobilization of 400,000 or 500,000 men and their absorption into the national activities of this country. Do hon. gentle-

men realize what the task of demobilizing such a force will mean? Do they realize what a task it will be to transport these men across the Atlantic? If we bring them across the Atlantic at the rate of a thousand *a day, if a steamer sails every day, accommodating a thousand of these men, it will take more than a year to bring them back to Canada. Further than that, it would be a very difficult task to absorb them into their former activities in this country if we attempted it at a much greater rate than that.
Then there is the importance of considering the very large number of men at present engaged in the production of munitions in Canada. As I have already said, they number more than 300,000 men. We have the further problem before us of such immigration as may come to this country from Great Britain when the war is ended. It has been the experience, I believe, after former wars, that men have a tendency to go to a new country 'with the idea of having a different life, a newer life, an outdoor life and so it may be after this war. No one can predict with certainty; but we may have considerable immigration from the British Isles. Undoubtedly the British Government will desire to retain its people in the United Kingdom, and will make every reasonable provision and offer every reasonable inducement to that end. We must not attempt unduly to interfere with such a policy. But the British Government have another policy, which will commend itself to us; and it is this: if there is to be emigration from the British Islands, it should be the duty of the Government of the Mother Country and of the Governments of the overseas dominions to cooperate, so that this emigration may be to a country under our Flag, to one of the overseas dominions of the Empire. We have offered to co-operate, and we shall co-operate, with the British Government for that purpose. We shall also co-operate, and we have offered to co-operate, with the provincial governments of Canada for that purpose. There was a recent conference between the Federal Government and the provincial governments at which these matters were under consideration. The most important purpose that we can have before us with regard to British immigrants as well as our own soldiers returning from the front is that as many as possible of them should settle on the land. It will be the duty of the Dominion Government and of the provincial governments- and I know that they realize this duty-to offer such

assistance and such inducements as will make the settlement of these men upon the land a success. That is one of the subjects which I hope to have an opportunity of discussing when I visit Great Britain this winter. I know that any measures which may be taken by the Federal Government for that purpose will have the hearty co-operation, as to purpose at least, of all hon. gentlemen in this House. We may differ as to details and as to methods, but I know there is no one on either side of the House who would not heartily join with the Government in any well devised effort to accomplish such a result.
I shall come in a moment to some of the more direct observations of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, but before doing so, I shall say a word with reference to the paragraph in His Excellency's speech respecting the extension of the Parliamentary term during the period of the war. I do not purpose to argue that question to-night; it would be undesirable that 1 should do so after what has fallen from my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I simply desire to put my view in a very few words. I stated the reasons for the proposal last year, and as far as my comprehension goes, the reasons which I then advanced are equally cogent to-day. I stated to the House at that time the view which had been taken by the press of the country, the view which had been expressed by certain hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, the view which had been expressed in very cogent terms indeed by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, when he emphasized the very great undesirability of having an election during the progress of the war. He went so far, if I remember his language correctly, as to say that while he did not have the greatest possible confidence in the Government of the day he never intended to open the portals of office with a bloody key. Well, the casualties and the perils to-day are not such as to make that observation any less cogent now than it was then. I should like to express one thought I did not express last year, and have hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House take it into account, and it is this: I was at the front in the summer of 1915. Before a general election can take place we shall have perhaps 200,000 or 250,000 or 300,000 men in France. I know something of the conditions at the front, and I venture to put this thought before the House and the
country: the men at the front will be not only practically, but actually, disfranchised if an election does take place in this country while they are in the trenches. That is my conviction. I say they would be actually disfranchised because, although I render every tribute to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the committee which had in hand the preparation of the Soldiers Voting Act of 1915, I am not disposed to think that the arrangements made in that Act or in any other act that could be devised aTe such as to enable those men to vote, or at least any considerable number of them. You cannot predict what conditions may exist. Suppose an election came on in this country when the fiercest drive of the war was taking place. Do you imagine that the paymasters of those regiments and their commanding officers could busy themselves with handing out ballots to men whose souls were engrossed and whose lives were at stake in the enterprise in which they were engaged? There is something more than that. These men at the front have it not in their disposition-	[DOT]
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I say that those men at the front have it not in their heart or their soul to consider matters of party controversy under the conditions with which they are there confronted. I believe those men would want to put aside any one who came to talk to them about political issues or partisan controversy, under conditions of life or of death, of victory or of defeat such as confront them in the trenches or while making a drive to bring this war to an end. Further than that, there may be perhaps a hundred thousand men not in France. You might be able to have some of those men vote for Government or for Opposition, not for a candidate, as provided in the Act alluded to; but do you imagine" that those men who are putting their lives to the supreme test in going overseas to fight for their country, will be greatly interested in political issues, or that they will desire to hear political speeches, or that they will welcome the distribution of partisan literature? I am not saying whether or not these considerations should determine the issue, but I do say that they are considerations that must be taken into account by every member of this parliament when upon him the responsibility falls as to whether or not there shall be a general election during this war, and I leave it at that.

My right lion, fiiend has not spoken of the proposal that we should celebrate in Canada the anniversary^ of a half century of Confederation. I do not propose, nor do I think any member of this House would propose that there should be <any spectacular celebration or any considerable expenditure of public money. The celebration should be a grave and serious one, having regard to the great trial through which Canada and the Empire is passing; but it seems to me that it is too notable an event to be permitted to pass without adequate commemoration. When we think of all that has been accomplished in this country in the past fifty years, we have reason to be proud, and to be grateful, and to be humble as well: proud of what' has been accomplished; grateful for the magnificent heritage with which Providence has endowed us, and humble because of the very great responsibility that the vastness of that heritage and our duty towards it bestow upon us. And so we should approach the celebration of this anniversary in a reverent spirit. The four scattered, disconnected, disunited provinces have become a mighty nation which has thrown into this war a spirit and an effort that have invested Canada with a new dignity before the world. The fiftieth anniversary of our national life will arrive while we are passing through events, the greatness of wihich surpasses the most vivid imagination. Those events have already profoundly influenced the spirit of our people. They are continuing so to influence it. We begin to realize, perhaps as never before, that, notwithstanding all our resources, notwithstanding all our material development, notwithstanding all our production and all our wealth, we may be weighed in the balance and found wanting if .the character and ideals of the people are not maintained.. So I say, it is with a grave and reverent, but with a firm and steadfast spirit that Canada should approach the celebration of her fiftieth anniversary.
I come now in the way of criticism to some of the observations in which my right hon-friend the leader of the Opposition has indulged this afternoon. He is 9 p-m. sure the soldiers have done well;
he is not so sure the Government has done well. I understand he expressed himisalf elsewhere in even .stronger terms than that, because I think that, at least at one meeting in which he was assisting in proposals for recruiting, he began his observations by emphasizing his lack of confidence in the Government. I do not think r Sir Robert Borden. 1
that is a very inspiring topic to enlarge upon at a recriiiting meeting, nor do I think a recruiting meeting would be inspired by emphasizing the fact that Great Britain had not come to the aid of France in 1870. We all, however, have our ideas, on such matters, and the course taken by my right hon. friend in that regard seemed to commend itself to him. He doubts whether the Government has done well, and he observes that the answer is to be found in certain correspondence that has been made .public. He declares that there has been lack of unity and continual jarring and disputing, and he .arrives at the conclusion that the interest of the country and the prosecution of the war have suffered materially through that fact. My right hon. friend has had some experience and he can speak with .authority on the subject, because we recollect tnat one of the most prominent colleagues in his own cabinet used to declare publicly, speaking of himself and his colleagues, that they fought like blazes. My right hon, friend is not unaware, of the fact that in any cabinet, however constituted, there may be differences of opinion, and that there must be differences of temperament. He seems to find a considerable amount of fault with myself as .head of the Government, because be arrives at the conclusion that I have not enough firmness or enough decision. In the course of my public life I have seen some instances which might prevent my right hon. friend from putting his head in the air and talking in that somewhat boastful way, because he evidently intended to institute a comparison between the weakness and lack of decision in the present head of the Government and the firmness and decision which prevailed while he was at the head of the Government. In 1902 I observed in the House of Commons a spectacle which I never saw- before, nor do I think that any one else ever saw the like; and that was when his most important colleague in the Government arose in his place in Parliament and openly flouted him to his face, taunting him with his failure to implement his pledges with regard to free trade. The colleague to whom I allude was Sir Richard Cartwright, and if any one doubts it, let him turn to the Hansard of 1902 and observe the statement which Sir Richard Cartwright made on that occasion, My right hon. friend speaks of firmness and decision and the lack of it at present. I did not observe that there was any great firmness or decision on the part of my"right hon. friend when it became a ques-

tion as to what Canada should do to aid the Empire in the South African war. The first pronouncement of my right hon. friend was' that not a man nor a gun should go.

And not a dollar
spent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Practically that.
I will not say that is the language, but it was an announcement to the country which produced such an outburst that my right hon. friend, notwithstanding his firmness and decision, came to the conclusion that men should go, and men did go to the extent in two years of about five thousand, the British Government being called upon to undertake their maintenance and support after they left the shores of Canada. That did not end the matter. There were two factions, and the other faction becoming restless under those conditions, my right hon. friend was obliged, in order to placate it, to pass am order in council -that this should not be construed as a precedent that Canada was to take any part in the future wars of the Empire. And having said that no men should go, and then afterwards having consented that some men should go' provided that Great Britain undertook to maintain them after they left our shores, and *thereafter having declared by order in council that this should not be regarded as a precedent, my right hon. friend seems to think that on that occasion he gave an illustration of what firmness and decision should be.
When this war broke oiit, and before my colleagues had assembled in Ottawa, I took upon myself the responsibility of saying to the British Government that Canada would stand in this war to the end with the British' Empire. That was my decision then; and I was ready to stand or fall by it, I am ready to stand or fall by it to-day.
I do not want to waste very much time over the question of who has the most firmness or the most decision, but I am perfectly willing to compare records with my right hon. friend in that regard. The order in council was passed, as I have said, that it should not bt, a precedent. Well, I am bound to ,say, it was not a precedent for mie. I took the ground that Canada would not only throw herself into this struggle to the full extent of her energies in support of the Empire and of all that the Empire means to the world, but that we should maintain our men at the front and thus bear our share-that Canada would keep up her own expeditionary force. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham)
was good enough to pay his respects to me also on this subject and to allude to the head of the Government as a very weak and undecided person; and to explain that if the leader of the Opposition had been in my place he would have called up the Minister of Militia and Defence on the telephone .and dismissed him.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, something very much of that kind.

I said he would have
called the Minister of Militia and Defence to the office, and if he could not give a reasonable explanation, would have dismissed him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Graham) must realize that the leader
of his Government may perhaps have treated him in one way while he treated more important colleagues in another way. He did not deal with Sir Richard Cartwright, nor Sir Oliver Mowat, nor Sir Henri Joly, nor the Hon. W. S. Fielding, in that way. If my hon. friend is speaking from experience, none of us has reason to doubt his word. " No unity of thought or action " says the right hon. gentleman. I do not think there has been less unity of thought or action in this Administration than there was in that over which my right hon. friend presided. I want to tell him that so far as I am concerned, I 'have been loyal to every one of my colleagues, and every one of my colleagues, so far as I know and as I most thoroughly and sincerely believe, has been loyal to me. So far as the late Minister of Militia and Defence is concerned, I gave him my loyal support, I gave him, I believe, as free a hand in connection with the conduct of the war as any other minister ever had or as. any could desire. I supported him in every possible way. And if he is under an impression to the contrary, 'he is under a wrong impression.
The criticism to which the leader of the Opposition addressed himself was that there was no immediate decision as to Canadian or British Control. Control of what? Our men at the front are under a British officer, Sir Douglas Haig. They are immediately under Sir Julian Byng. So far as control and direction of them as a military body is concerned, they must, of course, be under the same control and direction as the Test of the British forces. So far as promotions and appointments at the front are concerned, these should necessarily come with the sanction, approval, and

recommendation of the higher officers in command. It would be a dangerous and unfortunate course for this Government to undertake by interference in such matters to hamper or impede military operations.
What about our forces while in Great Britain?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I understand it, the control there has been maintained in Canada. The difficulty of the late Minister of Militia and Defence, so far as I remember, was owing to an order in council, which, it appeared, had not been brought to his attention and by which the Canadian officer commanding in England had greater powers than the Minister of Militia and Defence thought reasonable. When he brought the subject to the attention of Council, an order in council was passed amending it, and the order in council so passed remained in force up to the time he went out of office.
And also in France. Under the order in council that was rescinded, the officer commanding in France, General Alderson, had absolute authority.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not propose to enter into a discussion as to whether he was right or wrong. There was an order in council to which the late Minister of Militia and Defence took exception, thinking that he should have more control, and it was amended upon his initiative and recommendation so as to give him increased control over appointments both in Great Britain and in France.
Now, I desire to say a word as to equipment. In the early months of the war, a difficulty naturally arose because the transport and equipment were not of precisely the same type as those in Great Britain as I understand it-and, of course, I speak without the intimate knowledge of such matters po.sses.sed by the officers of the department, and, doubtless, by my hon. friend, the late Minister of Militia and Defence. It is important for an army a? the front to have a uniform standard of equipment, transport, and everything else. Otherwise, it is necessary to have supplies of the different types of transport and equipment in the ordnance stores behind the front, and this is a hindrance to military operations. I believe that some equipment supplied was left when the first Canadian contingent departed for France. I have spoken of that in this House before.

I discussed, the matter with General Carson when I was in England last year. He told me that the equipment was left because it was not of the same type as the British equipment and they .did not desire to have two types. He took what seemed a proper and reasonable course. He called a board, on which both Canada and Great Britain were represented, for the purpose of inquiring whether this equipment had been left because it was not a good equipment or because it was not uniform with the other. He told me that the board declared that it was good equipment. And it was taken over and used in the British Islands, and Canada received full credit for the value of it. It is most desirable, if the troops from Canada and from the rest of the Empire are to fight side by side, that all equipment and transport should be standardized, for it is obvious that otherwise operations cannot be carried on so effectively. It might have been better if that matter had been taken into consideration. before the war. It was not taken into consideration under the administration of my right hon. friend. I am not saying that by way of reproach, because I suppose no one could have anticipated war upon so tremendous a scale in which Canada would be called upon to take so great a part.
I believe that not only with respect to equipment but with respect to arms, guns and ammunition' as well as the Mother Country and the great dominions of the Empire ought to confer and co-operate and select uniform types, and that these types ought to be produced not only in the United Kingdom but in every one of the great dominions of the Empire. I hope also that a rifle to be called the Imperial service rifle may be adopted by the Mother Country and each of the great dominions after necessary expert examination and after consultation between the military authorities of Great Britain and the overseas dominions, so that in the future, in case the need for participation in war should arise, we should not have occasion to discuss differences in arms, transport, equipment or any other matter.
My right hon. friend read some portions of this correspondence; I shall not allude to that very much further. He referred to some remarks with regard to the Military Hospitals Commission, the Pensions Commission and the National Service Commission which had been made by my hon. friend the late Minister of Militia and Defence. So far as the Military Hospitals Commission is concerned, I do not think

there is any absurdity connected with that. As I have already pointed out, it was established upon the initiative of the exminister himself. If there is any absurdity connected with the Pensions Commission, it is an absurdity that must be visited upon the whole House of Commons, because that Pensions Commission was appointed upon the report of a committee of this House, unanimously affirmed by the vote of this House. As to the National Service Commission, at the time the observations were -made it had not really gone into operation at all. My right hon. friend states that he desires to discuss that commission on some other occasion. I shall be very happy to have him do so and to go into the matter fully then.
With respect to the alleged interference of the Canadian High Commissioner in military affairs, I am not aware of any such interference. I have telegraphed him from time to time asking him to get into communication with the War Office in respect of matters that required the co-operation of the two governments, and whenever I have asked him to do this he has done it. Outside of that, I am not aware that he has personally interfered at all. So far as Lord Kitchener's opinion is concerned, I note what my hon. friend read from the correspondence, but certainly I can say that in my interview with Lord Kitchener in 1915 he never expressed any such opinion to me.

The date to which reference was made was in October, 1914, when Lord Kitchener expressed himself as of the opinion that these troops were British regulars. Will the First Minister not say that I informed him immediately on my return to Canada on that subject?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have no recollection of it.
Of my telling the right hon. gentleman what Lord Kitchener and the High Commissioner-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I really have no recollection of it. I do not say it did not occur; I really have no recollection of it. I am only saying that in his consultation with me Lord Kitchener did not express any such opinion, nor did I find on the part of the War Office or on the part of any of the officials over there any desire to override Canada or Canadian interests. I can say that most sincerely; I have never discovered on the part of the British Government, the British War Office or any of the officials with whom I came in touch over there a
disposition to override or to disregard Canadian interests.
May I ask another question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly.
Has the First Minister a recollection of an objection being made to Colonel Steele, now General Steele, commanding the Second Division?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have a recollection of a question being raised as to whether his years were not so advanced that he could not stand the work at the front, and I have a recollection also that my hon. friend concurred in that view.
If the right hon. First Minister wants me to give an explanation, I can do it, but not now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will have to make, of course, any explanation he may see fit. I certainly understood him at the time to concur in that view.
The correspondence will show it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know what the correspondence shows; I have not looked at it. It is certainly my recollection that my hon. friend concurred in that view. Every one realizes the great ability and the splendid record of General Steele as a soldier. The only question raised to me from first to last, so far as I remember, was as to whether his years were not so advanced that it would be putting too much upon him to entrust him with the command which has been alluded to.

Perhaps it would be just as well if I should set it right now. At the time Colonel Steele was selected to command the Second Division positive objection were made to him that he was unfit- whether it was the question of his age or not. After he had a severe fall from his horse 'and had one shoulder broken, and after another injury at Shorncliffe, when the question of going over with the division was up, that was the time I agreed that General Steele was not physically fitted to go. Up to that time I had maintained that he was qualified to go.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did not charge my mind with these details. The distinct impression I had was that when the time came to appoint an officer in command of that division my -hon. friend the late Minister of Militia and Defence concurred in the

view that it would not be prudent or fair to General Steele to ask him to accept that command.
With regard to British officers scrapping equipment merely for the reason that it was Canadian, not British, I am not disposed to think that anything of the kind could have taken place. I believe that if any of our equipment was put to one side it was for the reason that uniformity in equipment was necessary at the front. If any incidents of a contrary nature ever occurred I cannot recall them at the moment. So far as I am concerned, there has not been in the past, nor will there be in the future any failure to uphold Canadian interests in every respect in connection with this war. On the other hand, I do not propose, I have not proposed in the past, and I do not propose in the future to set up my judgment or the judgment of this Government against the opinion of military experts who may say that it is necessary- that the type of equipment, of transport, or of anything else necessary in this war ought to be uniform and that the war cannot be carried on effectively unless it is uniform. If the military authorities, men of experience and good judgment in that regard, reach that conclusion, certainly I do not purpose setting up my judgment against it. Subject to that, I am sure that the members of this House and the people of this country may be satisfied that all Canadian interests in this war will be thoroughly upheld by those who are responsible for the administration of affairs to-day.

I am very much interested, apart from the question of difference between the late hon. Minister of Militia and the right hon. gentleman, in knowing exactly, in the interests of the men overseas, who are the controlling forces today with regard to promotions, appointments and other matters affecting the men overseas in Great Britain before they go across to France.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So far as I understand, the recommendations would come in the ordinary way from the commanding officers, and the overseas minister would recommend them to the Governor in Council, and they would be gazetted accordingly.

Then Sir George
Perley has control?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He would receive the recommendation of his officers, and make his recommendations to the Governor in Council; that is as I understand it.

Then the Canadian
Minister of Militia has nothing to do with it; it is directed entirely by Sir George Perley?	-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It would be dealt with by Sir George Perley because the forces over there are under his direction, and he has the same duties in regard to them as the Minister of Militia has in regard to the forces in Canada. There is, of course, wherever necessary, consultation and co-operation.
My right hon. friend has spoken of the war conference, and he has suggested a possible constitutional difficulty- I am bound to say that I do not know precisely what that can be. The War Cabinet, I suppose, could call to their conference any member of the Privy Council- The British Cabinet has called members of the Privy Council who are not members of the Government to their deliberations. I believe there was a precedent for that many years ago. There was a precedent for it in 1915. There was a precedent for it in 1916. I attended a meeting of the British Cabinet in 1915. Mr. Hughes of Australia attended several meetings, I believe, in 1916, and the fact that the present British Cabinet is a small Cabinet, a so-called War Cabinet, does not in any way raise a constitutional difficulty. My right bon- friend has alluded to the wide scope of the conference, to the wide scope of the subjects which are to be discussed at the conference; and certainly they have an exceedingly wide scope. It is for that reason that I sent the telegram which my right hon. friend has read. The subjects to be discussed are: first, urgent questions relating to the prosecution of the war; second, the conditions upon which the allied governments may assent to its termination; and thirdly, the problems which will then immediately arise. There really seems to be little left out of it; the prosecution of the war, the terms upon which peace may be made, and the problems that will then immediately arise. Because the scope was so comprehensive I asked for more information. It has not yet arrived. If it should be of a character that may properly be laid on the table of the House, I shall have no hesitation whatever in acquainting the House with its purport.
My right honourable friend has alluded to the arrangements that may be made in connection with my visit. It is difficult to say at the moment just what the best arrangement might be. On the one hand, I should not desire, if it could be avoided, to

put the members of this House to the inconvenience of a summer session. On the other hand, I thoroughly appreciate the spirit which my right, hon. friend has shown in making the suggestion which he has been good enough to lay before me, and I thank him very sincerely for it. I think it is a very considerate proposal on his part, and he may be sure that I shall take it into account, and consult with him respecting it. It seems to me that there can be no reasonable objection to it, but, on the spur of the moment, I cannot speak very definitely in that regard, and I should require to consult my colleagues with reference to it. It is perhaps desirable during an important session such as this, when measures of a very grave nature are to be proposed, that. the Prime Minister of the country should be present while these matters are under discussion. Without desiring to attach any undue importance to my presence here, I believe that honourable gentlemen will see some force in- the suggestion which my right hon. friend has made. On the other hand, I do not see that it would be at all proper for me to refuse the call to attend this conference. How useful it may be, remains to be determined in the future; but the call having come, I feel that one in my position must obey it without a moment's hesitation, putting aside all other considerations. And so it may be that the members of this House will have to be put to some inconvenience. I am sure that, if that inconvenience should arise, they will not take it into great ac- count, considering the hardships, the sacrifices that are being made by hundreds of thousands of our own countrymen in the effort to win this war.
With respect to the questions that are to be discussed, it is apparent to my right honourable friend, as it must be to all the members of this House, that I cannot give much information as to the determinations which may be reached. With regard to the prosecution of the war, I can give the conference this firm assurance:	that the
people of this country are united in their determination to throw all their efforts into the war, and to bring it to that conclusion which alone can bring about a lasting peace.
As to the conditions of peace, the second subject mentioned, my right hon. friend has expressed his opinion with regard to their general character. I am satisfied, and I think the people of this country will be satisfied, to abide by the conclusion
which has already been announced by the British Government, that peace will only be granted upon the condition of reparation for the past and guarantees for the _ future. It is quite impossible for those responsible for this war 'to make reparation in the highest or fullest sense. Of course, they cannot make reparation to the allied nations, nor indeed to their own people, for all the lives that have been lost, for all the blood that has been shed in their attempt to dominate the world. More than that, I do not suppose that it would be possible for the resources even of the great German nation to make reparation for all the material injury that has been caused in this war. I do not believe that that would be possible; but certain reparation must come. It must come to those people in Belgium who have seen their whole country desolated and devastated. It must come to those people in Belgium who by the hundred thousand have been dragged from their homes into practical slavery under conditions that have shocked the conscience of the whole world and are arousing the most intense feeling among neutral nations to-day. They must make reparation to Serbia. They must make reparation to those countries that they have devastated and desolated, and so far as may be possible-I do not say how far this may be possible-they ought to make reparation for the material losses suffered by those countries whose territory has not been invaded.
First there must be reparation for the past and then guarantees for the future. I absolutely agree with what my right hon. friend said this afternoon, and what 1, myself have said more than once, that all the sacrifices that we have made, all the blood that has been shed, all the treasure that has been poured out, would not only be in vain but would be absolutely worse than useless, if we did not bring about a peace with such guarantees as will ensure the world against any such aggression in the future. I say more than that. I say that not only the allied nations but all the neutral nations of the world are profoundly and deeply interested in the conclusion of a peace such as that. You cannot carry on a war under modern conditions which does not touch the whole world. Modern means of communication have brought the whole world together and no nation, no continent, can in future be a hermit. A great world devastating war like this is bound to affect profoundly not only the countries that are engaged in it but neutral nations as well. Therefore, it is to the absolute interest of

That is the only kind of peace that will be -of use to the world, to civilization, to humanity. I have spoken of the interests of the allied nations, I have spoken of the interests of the neutral nations, I will go farther than that, and say that no peace would be of any advantage to Germany herself unless it was a peace of that character and secured by such guarantees. In the interest of the whole world, it is essential that this peace shall be upon an absolutely permanent foundation and that aiT assurance shall be given not only to the allied nations but to all neutral nations, to humanity and to civilization itself that such attempts at aggression and world domination shall not be renewed in the future. If I go from you with any mandate, I believe I go from you with that mandate to the British Islands and to the allied nations.
We heard only the other day of a suggestion by Germany that there should be a round table conference at the Hague to bring the war to a conclusion, without any proposals as to terms to be discussed, without any proposition whatever except that there should be a conference. Sir Edward Grey pleaded, almost begged for a conference before this war broke out. What was the answer? You know the answer that was given by the German Emperor. The like answer that was given by the Austrian government.
